name: Gladstone's Land
description: From the narrow Lawnmarket pavement, Gladstone's Land rises six full storeys above you, its ground-floor arcade recreating the timber shopfronts that once lined the whole Royal Mile before Victorian street-widening swept the rest away. The building beside you began around 1550, but it was the merchant Thomas Gledstanes and his wife Bessie Cunningham who rebuilt it from 1617, raising it to its present height and finishing by 1620 with the elaborately painted ceilings still visible inside. By the 1930s the Old Town had emptied out and the house faced demolition — the National Trust for Scotland saved it just in time, reopening it after a further £1.5 million refurbishment in 2021.

name: The Hub
description: Glance up at the corner of Castlehill and Johnston Terrace and you'll find Edinburgh's tallest spire, 71.7 metres of dark neo-Gothic stone piercing the skyline above you. Queen Victoria laid the foundation stone here in 1842 for Victoria Hall, a joint design by Scottish architect James Gillespie Graham and English Gothic Revival master Augustus Pugin, built to give the Church of Scotland's General Assembly a proper meeting place. It became Highland Tolbooth St John's Church in 1929, holding Gaelic and English services until closing in 1979 and standing empty for over a decade. A five-year, £7.5 million restoration — one of the most complex conservation projects ever undertaken in Scotland — reopened it in 1999 as The Hub, home of the Edinburgh International Festival.

name: Camera Obscura & World of Illusions
description: Inside, the top floor still does exactly what it did in 1853: a rotating mirror throws a live, moving image of the city outside onto a table in front of you — one of the oldest working camera obscuras in Britain. Getting here took a scandal: Maria Theresa Short arrived in Edinburgh in 1827 claiming to be the daughter of instrument-maker Thomas Short, who had died nearly 40 years before, a claim never proven but enough to win her his prized telescope. She opened an observatory on Calton Hill in 1835, was forced out by the council in 1849, and reopened here on Castlehill in 1853 as Short's Observatory. After her death, the pioneering planner Patrick Geddes took over in 1892, renaming it the Outlook Tower and stacking its floors with views of the world, Europe, Scotland and Edinburgh in ascending order beneath the camera obscura at the top.

name: The Witchery by the Castle
description: Push through the door at Boswell's Court and candlelight closes around you — Gothic stone and low ceilings inside a merchant's townhouse raised in 1595 for Thomas Lowthian, later nicknamed for the eccentric physician Dr John Boswell, whose relatives James Boswell and Samuel Johnson once dined here. By the 1970s it had decayed into disused Church of Scotland committee rooms, until 20-year-old chef James Thomson bought it in 1979, becoming Scotland's youngest licensee at a time nobody rated the Royal Mile as restaurant territory. He expanded into the candlelit Secret Garden dining room in 1989, then into nine Gothic hotel suites, one entered through a hidden bookcase door. The name honours the hundreds burned as witches just up the street on Castlehill — locals still swear the building itself is haunted by one of them.

name: The Scotch Whisky Experience
description: You're standing in a former Victorian school building right beside the Castle esplanade. For over three decades visitors rode through 300 years of whisky history inside mock oak barrels, past theatrical sets built by the team behind York's Jorvik Viking Centre, before a 2023 renovation retired the ride for three new galleries: Origins, The Art of Whisky Making and Maturation. The place exists because in 1988 whisky executive Alastair McIntosh persuaded nineteen Scotch companies to put up £2 million so visitors who couldn't reach the Highlands could still learn the spirit's history. Since 2009 it's also housed one man's obsession: 3,384 bottles gathered over 35 years by Brazilian collector Claive Vidiz, now a Guinness World Record holder for the largest Scotch whisky collection on Earth, its oldest bottle dating to 1897.

name: Tartan Weaving Mill
description: A viewing window over the basement workshop lets you watch a working heritage loom weave tartan cloth in real time — a rare working link to what this building actually was: Castlehill Reservoir, built in 1849-50 to supply the New Town with water. The huge cistern could hold two million gallons and empty it at 5,000 gallons a minute; workmen digging its foundations in 1851 turned up two oak log-coffins and a Roman coin of the Emperor Constantine, relics of the earlier Christ Church chapel demolished on this same spot to help build the Tron Kirk. Drained in 1992, it opened briefly for public tours the following year before being converted between 1995 and 1997 into what's now the Tartan Weaving Mill.

name: Cannonball House
description: The west-facing wall here still holds an iron cannonball still lodged in the stone — legend says it was fired from the Castle's Half Moon Battery at Bonnie Prince Charlie during the 1745 Jacobite rising. It's a better story than the truth: engineers most likely fixed it there around 1675 to mark the exact height gravity-fed water from springs at Comiston needed to reach before it could flow this far up the hill, Edinburgh's first piped water supply. The Category A listed house itself was built in 1630 for furrier Alexander Mure and his wife Margaret Niellems, their initials still carved above the door as 'AM MN 1630'. It later became a Castlehill School annexe in 1913, then an urban studies centre, before the Contini family turned it into a restaurant in 2014.

name: Ramsay Garden
description: From below, Ramsay Garden's towers and white-harled walls seem to grow straight out of the castle rock — one of the most photographed skylines in Edinburgh, and one you can only admire from the street, since it's still private housing. It began in 1733 as an octagonal house built by the poet and wig-maker Allan Ramsay the Elder, its odd shape earning it the nickname 'the goose-pie house'. In 1890 the planner and biologist Patrick Geddes bought the site and rebuilt it as a deliberately mixed community of students, artisans and professionals, part of his campaign to drag Edinburgh's decaying Old Town back to life. Architect Stewart Henbest Capper designed the sixteen-apartment complex; Sydney Mitchell finished it after Capper's health failed. Geddes himself called the result 'the seven-towered castle I built for my beloved'.

name: Castle Esplanade
description: This broad, flat expanse opens out to views north to the Firth of Forth and south to the Pentland Hills — free to take in without a Castle ticket. It was built in 1753 as a military parade ground, using spoil dug from the foundations of the Royal Exchange down on the High Street, then widened and given its present north wall and railings in 1816. Every August since 1950 it's been transformed into the site of the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo — the first show had just eight items and drew 6,000 spectators to a single performance, compared with the roughly 10,000-seat temporary stadium built and dismantled here each summer today.

name: Edinburgh Castle
description: You're standing on the plug of an extinct volcano — Castle Rock has made this one of the most defensible sites in Scotland since at least the Iron Age, when a hillfort stood here some 3,000 years ago. It became a royal residence under King Malcolm III in the 11th century and was besieged more often than almost any fortress in Britain, including a night in 1314 when Thomas Randolph, Earl of Moray, led a party scaling the crag in darkness to recapture it from English hands. Today it holds the Honours of Scotland — the crown jewels — and the Stone of Destiny, used for centuries in Scottish coronations, though persistent rumour holds that the monks of Scone hid the real stone from Edward I and that what sits here is a substitute.

name: The Witches' Well
description: Set into the wall at the foot of the esplanade, this small bronze relief marks Edinburgh's principal witch-burning ground, where an estimated 300 people were put to death on this spot alone. Patrick Geddes commissioned it in 1894 from his friend John Duncan, a leading figure of the Scottish Celtic Revival, fixing it to the wall of what was then the newly built Castlehill Reservoir. Look closely at the relief: a serene face and a wicked one, both entwined by a serpent coiled around Hygieia, Greek goddess of health, and her father Asclepius, god of medicine, with a sprig of foxglove worked in beside them — a heart medicine and a poison in one plant, a reminder that the same knowledge could heal or condemn whoever held it.

name: The India Cross
description: Trace the carving on this dark Celtic cross and among the entwined cable-work you'll find a stag's head and an elephant — the badge of the 78th Highlanders, raised here in 1862 to the 256 men of the regiment who died relieving the besieged garrison at Lucknow during the Indian Rebellion of 1857-58. Indian soldiers had risen against British rule that June; when the 78th fought through the rebel lines to reach the city that September, the whole regiment was voted the Victoria Cross by ballot, a mechanism reserved for acts of collective gallantry too widespread to credit to one man. The relieving commander, General Henry Havelock, is said to have declared he'd 'never seen better conduct — I am not a Highlander, but I wish I was one.'

name: Scottish Horse Memorial
description: This granite Celtic cross, carved with a claymore and a bronze lion rampant, was raised in 1904-05 to the Scottish Horse, a yeomanry regiment recruited from Scotland, Australia and South Africa in 1900 to fight Britain's brutal guerrilla campaign against Boer commandos in the Second Boer War. Look closely at the names and you'll find something unusual for a monument of this era: Zulu scouts who served and died alongside the regiment are named here too, a rare instance of Black South African soldiers being formally commemorated on a colonial-era war memorial. An identical cross stands on Caledonia Hill in Johannesburg, where it became the official war memorial of the Transvaal Scottish regiment. The Scottish Horse itself was disbanded at Edinburgh Castle in 1902; its lineage carries on today in the Scottish and North Irish Yeomanry.

name: The Afghan Needle
description: This pink Peterhead granite needle behind iron railings catches the wind coming straight off the esplanade, standing 3.5 metres tall and listed Grade II* by Historic Environment Scotland. Raised by public subscription in 1882-83, it commemorates the 105 officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the 72nd Duke of Albany's Own Highlanders who were killed in action or died of wounds and disease during the First and Second Anglo-Afghan Wars of 1839-42 and 1878-80. Read down its base and every name is grouped by how the man died — a stark ledger of two of the 19th century's bloodiest colonial campaigns, designed by the Aberdeen firm MacDonald, Field & Company. Locals simply call it the Afghan Needle.

name: The Gatehouse
description: The drawbridge and the portcullis groove above the arch are still in full working order, but don't be fooled — the whole Gatehouse forming the Castle's grand entrance is Victorian, built in 1886-88 to give the fortress a more romantic approach befitting its status as a national monument. It was reportedly designed in some secrecy, since military authorities feared a cosmetic addition to a still-functioning garrison might draw public criticism. Flanking the archway in twin Gothic niches designed by architect Sir Robert Lorimer stand bronze statues of Robert the Bruce and William Wallace, added decades later in 1929 to mark the 600th anniversary of Bruce's death — a project so divisive it filled the Scottish press with argument throughout 1928 and 1929 before Thomas Clapperton and Alexander Carrick were finally chosen to sculpt the two figures.

name: Princess Louise's Fountain Memorial
description: The stone here is worn smooth and its bronze fittings have gone green with age, but look closely at the central panel and you can still make out a royal crown, a row of smaller crowns and an entwined monogram above twin drinking basins built into the esplanade wall. An inscription across the base names 'THE PRINCESS LOUISE'S ARGYLLSHIRE HIGHLANDERS' — a horse-trough and fountain erected in 1874 by the regiment, styled after their royal colonel-in-chief, Queen Victoria's daughter Princess Louise, Duchess of Argyll. The regiment itself took that name in 1881, when the 91st and 93rd Highlanders amalgamated. It's one of a cluster of regimental memorials dotted along the esplanade's edges.

name: Robert the Bruce Statue
description: In the left-hand niche beside the Gatehouse stands Robert the Bruce in bronze, crowned and armoured, an axe in one hand and a heraldic shield in the other — sculptor Thomas J. Clapperton's pose recalling Bruce's single combat with the English knight Henry de Bohun on the eve of Bannockburn in 1314, when he split de Bohun's skull with one blow while mounted on nothing grander than a small palfrey. Unveiled on 28 May 1929, the 600th anniversary of Bruce's death, the statue only exists because a public design competition over how to portray Scotland's two great medieval heroes turned unexpectedly divisive, filling the Scottish press with argument through 1928 and 1929 before a compromise split the commissions between Clapperton and his rival sculptor.

name: William Wallace Statue
description: In the matching niche to the right of the archway stands William Wallace, sculpted by Alexander Carrick in chainmail and plaid, gripping a claymore with a helmet resting at his feet — unveiled the same day, 28 May 1929, as his Bruce counterpart opposite. Wallace led the rebel Scottish army to a stunning victory over a much larger English force at Stirling Bridge in 1297 and was appointed Guardian of Scotland, only to be defeated the following year at Falkirk. Betrayed and captured in 1305, he was dragged to London and executed as a traitor to a crown he'd never sworn allegiance to — a death that only hardened Scottish resistance and helped set up Bruce's victory at Bannockburn sixteen years later.

name: Ensign Ewart Memorial and Grave
description: Beneath this granite memorial on the esplanade lies Charles Ewart, a Royal Scots Greys sergeant who fought off a standard-bearer, a lancer and an infantryman in quick succession at Waterloo in 1815 to capture the eagle standard of the French 45th Regiment — brutal hand-to-hand combat that made him a minor celebrity, promoted to Ensign and reportedly acquainted with Sir Walter Scott, though he claimed to shun the attention himself. He died in 1846 near Manchester and was buried in Salford, where the graveyard was later paved over and his grave forgotten. His remains were only rediscovered in the 1930s and reburied here with full military honours on 16 April 1938, nearly a century after his death.

name: James' Court
description: Off the Lawnmarket, James' Court is a place where the noise falls away — a quiet close of 18th-century tenements behind Gladstone's Land, built from 1723-27 by James Brownhill and, for a while, one of Edinburgh's most fashionable addresses. The philosopher David Hume lived here before decamping to the grander New Town, and the diarist James Boswell later rented Hume's old flat. It was here in 1773 that Boswell hosted Samuel Johnson during the very trip through Scotland that produced Johnson's 'A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland' — though the court Boswell knew burned down in 1857 and was rebuilt, so what stands around you now isn't quite the building the two men actually sat in.

name: The Jolly Judge
description: Duck down the stair below street level and the Jolly Judge opens out beneath low beamed ceilings and a roaring log fire — a hideaway just off the Lawnmarket that keeps its music off deliberately, a rarity on a Royal Mile otherwise full of noise. The pub's proximity to the Sheriff Court and High Court once made it a favourite with Edinburgh's legal community, hence the name. That quiet, unhurried approach has paid off: CAMRA named it Edinburgh Pub of the Year in both 2023 and 2024, on top of a run of Cider Pub of the Year awards for a cellar built around real ales and ciders rather than the usual tourist-trail lager.

name: Susannah Alice Stephen Memorial
description: Sit on this memorial bench in James' Court's small garden and above you perches a bronze parakeet beside a garden trug, sculpted by Frances Pelly for Susannah Alice 'Zannah' Stephen, a landscape designer who co-founded the Scottish Society of Garden Designers before her death in a diving accident off the Galapagos Islands in 1997. She chose this exact spot deliberately: Patrick Geddes, the town planner she admired for bringing green space into the Old Town's cramped closes, had once lived in James' Court himself. The memorial was unveiled in September 2000, its inscription reading 'Keep your face towards the sun and the shadows will fall behind you.'

name: The Ensign Ewart
description: Trading in some form since 1680, this is the highest pub on the Royal Mile and the closest one to the Castle gates — parts of the building are reckoned to go back even further, to around 1603. It carried a different name until 1938, when it was renamed for Ensign Charles Ewart of the Royal Scots Greys, whose eagle-capturing exploit at Waterloo in 1815 had just been marked by his reburial with full military honours on the Castle esplanade a few hundred metres from where you're standing. Inside, a large painting of the Battle of Waterloo hangs among Scottish military memorabilia, keeping Ewart's story on the walls of the pub that carries his name.

name: Boswell's Court
description: Above the stair entrance, a carved lintel still bears a merchant's mark and the initials 'T' and 'L', a signature left by Thomas Lowthian, the merchant who built this 17th-century townhouse in 1595. Despite the name, it wasn't James Boswell who lived here but his uncle, the physician Dr John Boswell — James did visit in October 1762, and a plaque on the building, now home to The Witchery restaurant, also claims he dined here with Samuel Johnson around 1770. Castlehill was already steeped in history by then: the Palace of Mary de Guise, mother of Mary Queen of Scots, is said to have once stood directly across the street.

name: Ramsay Lane
description: The cobbles pitch steeply as Ramsay Lane climbs from the Royal Mile up toward the Castle esplanade, named for the poet Allan Ramsay, whose octagonal home once stood at its head — nicknamed 'the goose-pie house' for its round-fronted shape. Ramsay built it in 1733 and retired there in 1740; his son, later court painter to George III, extended it eastward, and by 1890 the site had become the foundation for Ramsay Garden, the striking Arts and Crafts development that still lines the lane's upper end today.
